extracted.intended_audience: scholars, graduate students, and researchers studying administrative rulemaking, interest group mobilization, and methods for measuring public comment influence
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and measurement rules for identifying, clustering, coding, and modeling the influence of public comment campaigns and lobbying coalitions on federal rulemaking outcomes. Includes operational definitions, hand-coding protocols, inclusion/exclusion rules, and predictor/variable construction for quantitative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying success (five-point scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying Success—whether each comment got what it asked for in the change between a draft and final rule—is coded on a five-point scale from 2 to -2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘2’ indicates that most of the commenter’s requests were met; ‘-2’ indicates the rule moved decidedly in the opposite direction. Lobbying success is measured both at the specific-demand level and as an overall score per comment/organization/coalition. Coalition-level success uses the lead organization’s coding or the average across coalition members. The mean of hand-coded lobbying success on the {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2} scale is used as the dependent variable in models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a mass comment campaign
rubrics_metrics.description: If a coalition mobilizes more than 99 form-letter comments on a proposed rule, that coalition is coded as having a mass comment campaign (campaign = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The numeric measure 'mass comments' is the count of supportive comments mobilized by the campaign; models typically use the logged number or include a quadratic term to account for diminishing marginal impact. Where a coalition submits only technical comments and no mass mobilization, campaign and mass comments are 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clustering by text reuse (10-word phrase rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify comments that share ten-word phrases with 99 or more other comments to detect form letters and mass-comment text reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First remove all 10-word phrases that appear in the proposed rule (preamble and call for comments). Then find comments sharing ten-word phrases with >=99 other comments. Collapse such form-letter comments to one representative document for hand-coding. Empirically, a 10-word phrase repeated across more than a few comments is either text copied from the proposed policy or a campaign form letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of comment types (attachments vs textbox)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include all comments submitted as file attachments or emails; include textbox comments only if they share text with other comments (indicating part of a pressure campaign); exclude entirely unique textbox contents and comments shorter than ten words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sophisticated lobbying organizations almost always submit comments as file attachments; textbox comments are included when they are part of repeated text. Excluding unique textbox comments and <10-word comments reduces noise (e.g., trivial 'This sucks') while retaining form letters and substantive comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of comments to organizations/coaltions
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute each comment to the organization behind it (its author if submitted by the organization or the mobilizing organization for form letters) by extracting organization names from comment text and using internet searches when comments do not reference an organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-signed comments are assigned to the same coalition. Form-letter comments are assigned to the mobilizing organization/coalition. Use a combination of automated search methods and hand-coding to identify organizations and coalitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collapsing to organization/coalition observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Collapse data to one observation per organization or coalition per proposed rule for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because hypotheses are about organizations and coalitions, aggregate comments so each organization/coalition on a docket is a single observation. Identify the main substantive comment submitted by each organization (usually the longer staff/lawyer comment) for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition identification and coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify lobbying coalitions by hand and by textual similarity; co-signed comments and form letters belong to the same coalition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name a coalition typically after one of its lead organizations. Record coalition attributes including size (count of distinct commenting organizations), whether it is a coalition (indicator if size >1), whether it is business-led or non-business-led, and whether it is public-interest or private-interest majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coalition size
rubrics_metrics.description: Coalition size is a count of the number of organizations lobbying together on the rule (distinct commenting organizations); size = 1 for organizations lobbying alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coalition size as a predictor of lobbying success. Multiple coalitions may lobby the same rule; treat each coalition-rule pairing as a separate observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unopposed coalition indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition is unopposed when no opposing organizations comment on the same rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive opposition from hand-coded spatial positions of comments; unopposed status is used as a predictor of lobbying success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-coding protocol: content to record
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-coding includes recording the type of organization, the lobbying coalition to which each comment belongs, the type of coalition (primarily public or private interests), their policy demands, and the extent to which the change between the draft and final rule aligned with their demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each comment, coders identify the main overall policy demand, the top three specific demands, and the corresponding parts of draft and final rule texts. Several rules were double-coded; a codebook is provided (Appendix A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring lobbying success by commenter-defined demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure lobbying success by the degree of alignment between commenters’ stated demands and the change between draft and final rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach centers the analysis on issues commenters care about (the 'first face of power'), but may miss policy issues outside commenter attention. Alternatives (and their tradeoffs) include counting mentions in agency responses or using a priori policy dimensions (e.g., Balla et al.'s five factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial position collapse to support/opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Collapse the spatial position coding into a dichotomous indicator of whether a comment ultimately supports or opposes the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this binary indicator for things like determining whether a coalition is unopposed and for aggregate summaries; detailed spatial coding still used for finer-grained measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative document for repeated form letters
rubrics_metrics.description: For comments sharing repeated text, code one sample (representative) document for all versions of the form letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collapsing repeated texts reduces hand-coding workload by orders of magnitude while preserving the substance of mobilized messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main predictor construction: supportive comments count
rubrics_metrics.description: The main predictor variable is the number of supportive comments generated by a public pressure campaign (the tally of comments mobilized by each organization or coalition running a mass-comment campaign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because marginal impacts diminish, models typically use logged counts or include quadratic terms. Very large observed ranges (0 to >3 million) warrant transformation and robust modeling strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling repeated-administration dockets
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new administration uses the same docket number to solicit comments on a proposed rule previously used, count these as separate rulemaking dockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat repeated dockets separately because subsequent policies often reverse or move policy in an opposite direction; organizations may comment with opposite positions across administrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying organization-originated comments vs individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop software and methods to select comments most likely submitted by organizations (e.g., include file attachments, shared texts), excluding likely individual, trivial, or idiosyncratic textbox comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include textbox comments only if they share text with other comments; exclude very short comments (<10 words). This increases the likelihood of analyzing substantive organizational input and mass-mobilized text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis choice: coalition vs organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the lobbying coalition as the unit of analysis (rather than organization) to avoid counting one coalition's single campaign as many co-linear observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting organization-level campaigns as separate observations when they are part of the same coalition inflates non-independence; coalition-level analysis better reflects distinct policy contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative success measures and their tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss alternative measures of responsiveness: (1) count of mentions in the agency’s response to comments; (2) a priori policy dimensions (e.g., number of regulated entities, standards level, compliance deadlines, monitoring requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting mentions may be influenced by agencies' strategic responsiveness and counts explicit rejections as responsiveness. A priori dimensions may miss issues commenters emphasize. The chosen commenter-defined approach focuses on what commenters care about but may omit non-commenter public concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling strategy for hand-coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Random sample of 172 proposed rules with both a mass-comment campaign and a final rule; additional sample of 43 proposed rules where the same organizations commented without a mass comment campaign; sample weighted toward high-salience dockets and covers 60 agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sampling intentionally overrepresents high-comment, contentious rules because a simple random sample of all rules would yield few with pressure campaigns. Interpret statistical results as reflecting variation in high-salience rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding of coalition type (public vs private interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify coalitions as 'public interest' or 'private interest' based on whether the majority of organizations are non-businesses (governments and nonprofits) or businesses/trade associations; also track share_of_businesses as an objective measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two measures correlate but can diverge (e.g., public interest coalitions with many business allies). Estimate alternative models with each measure and use 'public/private' label as a qualitative indicator of coalition type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection and coding of comments from elected officials
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify comments submitted by members of Congress and count legislators in each lobbying coalition; record elected-official type (House, Senate, state, local, governor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislator comments are a distinct mechanism of influence; oversight letters are frequently co-signed. Count of legislator comments varies massively across agencies and rules and is used as a predictor/mediator of influence.
